Sharing results: tables, figures, reports and interactive graphics

Source: vignettes/reports.Rmd
reports.Rmd

An analysis ends in a manuscript, a report, a slide or a web page. This vignette shows how the tables and figures of a joinpoint fit get there: saved to files in the format each needs, written into a complete report, printed in R Markdown and Quarto documents, and drawn as interactive graphics.

The examples use the tuberculosis and stroke mortality of us_mortality:

library(joinpoint)
fit <- joinpoint(subset(us_mortality, cause %in% c("Stroke", "Tuberculosis")),
                 year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 3, ci_method = "parametric")
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "joinpoint-reports")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

Tables

jp_save() writes a table in the format given by the extension of the file: .csv, .tsv and .txt for spreadsheets and other software, .md for Markdown, .tex for LaTeX, and .docx, .odt, .rtf, .pptx, .html and .pdf for documents. A title becomes the caption, and a note is printed under the table:

tab <- jp_table(fit)
jp_save(tab, file.path(dir, "trends.tex"), title = "Trends in mortality",
        note = "* The APC or AAPC differs from 0 at alpha = 0.05.",
        label = "tab:trends")

The LaTeX table uses the rules of the booktabs package (\usepackage{booktabs} in the preamble) and escapes the special characters of LaTeX:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Trends in mortality}
\label{tab:trends}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
cause & Trend & Period & APC / AAPC (95\% CI) & p \\
\midrule
Stroke & Segment 1 & 1900-1945 & -0.94* (-1.06, -0.83) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Stroke & Segment 2 & 1945-1968 & -0.05 (-0.40, 0.30) & 0.757 \\
Stroke & Segment 3 & 1968-1987 & -4.68* (-5.13, -4.23) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Stroke & Segment 4 & 1987-1998 & -1.29* (-2.27, -0.30) & 0.011 \\
Stroke & AAPC & 1900-1998 & -1.51* (-1.68, -1.34) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Tuberculosis & Segment 1 & 1900-1947 & -3.72* (-3.91, -3.53) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Tuberculosis & Segment 2 & 1947-1954 & -14.66* (-18.35, -10.80) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Tuberculosis & Segment 3 & 1954-1981 & -8.97* (-9.41, -8.53) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Tuberculosis & Segment 4 & 1981-1998 & -4.52* (-5.39, -3.64) & $<$ 0.001 \\
Tuberculosis & AAPC & 1900-1998 & -6.14* (-6.50, -5.78) & $<$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\par\smallskip{\footnotesize * The APC or AAPC differs from 0 at alpha = 0.05.}
\end{table}

Any data frame can be saved this way, for example the APCs as numbers or the model selection statistics, with the decimals set by digits:

jp_save(apc(fit), file.path(dir, "apc.csv"))
jp_save(model_selection(fit)$criteria, file.path(dir, "selection.md"),
        digits = 2)

Word, OpenDocument, PowerPoint, RTF, HTML and PDF documents are made with Pandoc, which comes with RStudio and Quarto, through the rmarkdown package; PDF documents also need LaTeX (for example tinytex::install_tinytex()). A Word table for a manuscript:

jp_save(tab, file.path(dir, "trends.docx"), title = "Trends in mortality")

Figures

Figures are saved the same way: in the image formats of ggsave() (.png, .pdf, .svg, .tiff, .eps and others), as a LaTeX figure, or inside a Word, OpenDocument, PowerPoint or HTML document. width, height (inches) and dpi set the size and resolution:

g <- autoplot(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE)
jp_save(g, file.path(dir, "trends.png"), width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300)
jp_save(g, file.path(dir, "trends.tex"), title = "Mortality trends",
        label = "fig:trends")

The .tex file is a figure environment that includes a PDF of the figure written beside it (trends.pdf), ready for \input{} in a manuscript.

Complete reports

jp_report() writes the whole analysis: the settings in words, the table of APCs and AAPCs, the joinpoints, the model selection statistics and the figures. An .Rmd or .qmd file gives the R Markdown or Quarto source, with the fit saved beside it, ready to edit and render:

jp_report(fit, file.path(dir, "mortality.qmd"),
          title = "Trends in mortality", author = "A. Analyst")
---
title: "Trends in mortality"
author: "A. Analyst"
date: "2026-11-20"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(joinpoint)
fit <- readRDS("mortality_fit.rds")
```

## Analysis

The trend of Rate over Year was modeled by a log-linear joinpoint model with constant variance for each of 2 cohorts. The number of joinpoints (0 to at most 3) was selected by the weighted BIC; the selected models have 3 joinpoints. The tables give parametric confidence intervals at the 95% level, and the 95% level for the joinpoints. The intervals are conditional on the number of joinpoints.

## Annual Percent Changes

```{r}
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit), caption = "APCs of the segments and AAPCs, with 95% confidence intervals.")
```

## Joinpoints

```{r}
jt <- joinpoints(fit)

Other extensions give the rendered report: .html, .docx, .odt, .pdf, .md or .tex. The figures of HTML reports are interactive when the ggiraph package is installed.

jp_report(fit, file.path(dir, "mortality.docx"), title = "Trends in mortality")

jp_save() of a fit writes the same report.

Fits in R Markdown and Quarto documents

A fit printed in a chunk of an R Markdown or Quarto document shows the same summary as in the console. With the option joinpoint.knit_table, set once in the first chunk of the document, it appears instead as the table of jp_table(), formatted for the output (HTML, LaTeX, Word or Markdown); the chunk option tab.cap sets its caption:

options(joinpoint.knit_table = TRUE)
fit
Trends in stroke and tuberculosis mortality.
cause Trend Period APC / AAPC (95% CI) p
Stroke Segment 1 1900-1945 -0.94* (-1.06, -0.83) < 0.001
Stroke Segment 2 1945-1968 -0.05 (-0.40, 0.30) 0.757
Stroke Segment 3 1968-1987 -4.68* (-5.13, -4.23) < 0.001
Stroke Segment 4 1987-1998 -1.29* (-2.27, -0.30) 0.011
Stroke AAPC 1900-1998 -1.51* (-1.68, -1.34) < 0.001
Tuberculosis Segment 1 1900-1947 -3.72* (-3.91, -3.53) < 0.001
Tuberculosis Segment 2 1947-1954 -14.66* (-18.35, -10.80) < 0.001
Tuberculosis Segment 3 1954-1981 -8.97* (-9.41, -8.53) < 0.001
Tuberculosis Segment 4 1981-1998 -4.52* (-5.39, -3.64) < 0.001
Tuberculosis AAPC 1900-1998 -6.14* (-6.50, -5.78) < 0.001

Figures are drawn by autoplot() and the other plot functions as in any chunk.

Interactive graphics

Every figure of the package can be drawn as an interactive graphic, with interactive = TRUE in the plot function and jp_interactive(), or jp_interactive() on the fit directly. The graphic looks like the static figure. Hovering a segment shows its period, APC, confidence interval and p value and highlights the segment with its band and label; hovering an observation shows its value, its confidence interval and the fitted trend; hovering a joinpoint shows its location and confidence interval. The toolbar zooms and saves the graphic as an image.

jp_interactive(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE, height = 4.2)

The other figures are chosen with plot, here the APC of each segment:

jp_interactive(fit, plot = "apc", height = 3.5)

A figure changed with the grammar of ggplot2 stays interactive:

g <- autoplot(fit, interactive = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Mortality per 100,000", x = NULL)
jp_interactive(g, height = 4.2)

The graphics are htmlwidgets: they appear in the RStudio viewer, in HTML documents made with R Markdown or Quarto, on pkgdown sites and in Shiny applications (with ggiraph::girafeOutput() and ggiraph::renderGirafe()), and jp_save() writes them to a standalone web page:

jp_save(jp_interactive(fit), file.path(dir, "mortality.html"))

By default the text of the graphic uses fonts found on the computer that opens it, which keeps the page small; embed_fonts = TRUE embeds the fonts, so that the graphic looks exactly the same everywhere, at the cost of several megabytes.
